questions.question: Describe smallpox and the method of inoculation used before Jenner.
questions.expected_answer: Smallpox was an infectious disease spread through the air and by touching the sick or their things, causing high fever and painful blisters. It killed about three in ten of its victims and left many scarred or blind; in 1713 an epidemic at the Cape devastated the Khoikhoi. Before Jenner, people in Africa, India, China and the Middle East used inoculation, rubbing smallpox material into a scratch to cause a mild case and lifelong protection, but it was risky because some died and it could spread smallpox.

questions.question: Describe Jenner's experiment of 1796 and explain how vaccination works.
questions.expected_answer: Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox did not seem to catch smallpox. In May 1796, he took pus from cowpox sores on the hand of milkmaid Sarah Nelmes and put it into cuts on the arm of James Phipps, aged eight. James had a mild fever and recovered. Later Jenner inoculated him with smallpox, and he did not get ill. A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and fight a disease without the person suffering the disease. Jenner named it from vacca, meaning cow.

questions.question: Explain how smallpox was eradicated.
questions.expected_answer: At first some people opposed the vaccine, but it spread around the world within a few years, and many countries made vaccination compulsory. In 1967, the World Health Organization began a worldwide campaign, tracking down every case and vaccinating everyone around the sick person to stop the spread. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 smallpox was declared eradicated, the only human disease wiped out in this way.
